prompt.context: Your client, Delson, is a $20B hard drive company that manufactures and sells hard drives to OEMs (e.g., HP). OEMs sell computers and data systems to consumers and all kinds of businesses. The hard drive industry's profitability has been cyclical, and recently seen a decline due to increasing competition and slow sales in computers. Therefore, the CFO of Delson decided to acquire a start-up company, Small Storage Systems (SSS). SSS purchases hard drives and then manufactures and sells data storage equipment for large companies to store and manage data efficiently. Software solutions are included with the equipment.
prompt.question: The CFO meets the BCG Partner at a dinner and asks for advice: what issues should we be concerned about with the newly acquired start-up SSS? What should we do?

clarifying_info.q: How concentrated is the OEM market?
clarifying_info.a: There are few companies in the OEM space, but many hard drive manufacturers.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost structure of the hard drive industry?
clarifying_info.a: The hard drive industry has very high fixed costs. Major players have very thin profit margins and need to maximize utilization in order to stay profitable.

exhibits.title: SSS Profit Margin via Own Sales Force vs. OEM Channel
exhibits.shows: A table comparing two go-to-market options for SSS (Own sales force vs. OEM channel), showing list price, price to OEM, COGS, Sales expense, G&A expense, and resulting profit margin for each option.

exhibits.title: Delson Revenue and Profit Margin
exhibits.shows: A table of Delson's financial metrics broken down by total revenue, overall profit margin, Enterprise OEM-specific profit margin, Enterprise OEMs' share of total revenue, and top 3 Enterprise OEMs' share of total Enterprise OEM revenue.

rows: Enterprise OEMs' share of total revenue
Top 3 Enterprise OEMs' share of total Enterprise OEMs revenue
data.note: Top 3 Enterprise OEMs will switch to other drive manufacturers if Delson builds own sales force for SSS.

framework: Identify the primary challenge: how does SSS acquire customers, since Delson currently has no direct sales force for large enterprise clients
Assess go-to-market channels: build own sales force vs. leverage existing OEM relationships
Evaluate financial trade-offs between the two channel options using profit margin analysis
Assess strategic risk: some OEMs (Enterprise OEMs) also sell data systems and would become direct competitors if Delson builds its own sales force
Quantify the downside: calculate profit loss from Enterprise OEMs switching suppliers if Delson competes with them
Account for fixed-cost structure: loss of large customers may push the hard drive business into negative margin
Synthesize into a recommendation balancing SSS growth opportunity against core hard drive business risk

questions.prompt: How do you interpret Exhibit 1 and what are your insights?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note: (1) OEMs demand a 25% discount (price to OEM = 75% of list), leaving SSS only 7% margin via that channel vs. 15% via own sales force. (2) Despite the higher margin, building an own sales force from scratch is costly and risky given lack of experience. (3) Most critically, some OEMs are also 'Enterprise OEMs' that sell data systems to large businesses — if Delson builds its own sales force, it turns from supplier to direct competitor against those OEMs.

questions.prompt: With Exhibit 2, evaluate whether or not to build own sales force. Quantify the profit impact.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate the profit loss if the top 3 Enterprise OEMs switch to competing hard drive manufacturers, then determine how much SSS revenue via own sales force would be needed to compensate.

math.setup: Profit loss = Delson total revenue × Enterprise OEM share × Top-3 share × Enterprise OEM profit margin. Required SSS own-sales revenue × (own margin − OEM margin) = profit loss.
steps: Profit loss from top 3 Enterprise OEMs leaving: $20B × 20% × 40% × 10% = $160M
Margin advantage of own sales force over OEM channel: 15% − 7% = 8%
Required SSS own-sales revenue to compensate: X × 8% = $160M → X = $2B
As a brand-new start-up, SSS is unlikely to achieve $2B in revenue in its first year; therefore building own sales force is not advisable.
math.answer: SSS would need $2B in first-year sales to compensate the $160M profit loss — unrealistic for a start-up, so building an own sales force is not recommended.

questions.prompt: If SSS could somehow sell more than $2B in its first year, would that change your recommendation?
questions.guidance: Candidate should incorporate the high-fixed-cost structure of the hard drive business. Losing top 3 Enterprise OEMs removes $1.6B in revenue ($20B × 20% × 40%). Because the vast majority of hard drive costs are fixed, total costs remain near $18.8B while revenue drops to ~$18.4B, potentially turning the entire hard drive division unprofitable. The growth of an unpredictable start-up cannot justify risking the entire core business.

math.setup: Illustrative fixed-cost scenario: current total costs vs. post-OEM-loss revenue.
steps: Revenue after losing top 3 Enterprise OEMs: $20B − ($20B × 20% × 40%) = $20B − $1.6B = $18.4B
With highly fixed costs, total costs without top 3 Enterprise OEM business likely remain above $18.4B → negative hard drive margin.
math.answer: Even if SSS exceeds $2B in sales, the fixed-cost structure means losing top 3 Enterprise OEMs could push the entire hard drive business into negative margin — making own sales force construction unjustifiable.

recommendation: Delson should not build its own sales force for SSS because the financial and strategic risks to the core hard drive business outweigh the profit margin benefit.
SSS should go to market through the OEM channel, accepting the 7% profit margin, to preserve Delson's critical Enterprise OEM relationships.
Delson should focus on growing SSS incrementally without jeopardizing the $20B hard drive revenue base.
risks: SSS profit margin via OEM channel is only 7%, limiting the financial upside of the acquisition.
OEM channel growth depends on OEM willingness and sales effort, reducing Delson's control over SSS's growth.
The core hard drive business remains exposed to cyclical industry decline regardless of SSS's channel strategy.
next_steps: Negotiate favorable terms with OEM partners for distributing SSS equipment to minimize discount pressure.
Develop a longer-term roadmap for SSS to assess when (and if) it reaches the scale at which building a dedicated sales force becomes financially viable without threatening core OEM relationships.
Explore whether SSS's software capabilities can create differentiation that justifies a premium and improves the 7% OEM-channel margin over time.
